text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

A $25.6 million wire fraud. Not a single line of code hacked. Every "colleague" on the video call was an AI-generated ghost. In my latest piece for *The Hindu BusinessLine*, I examine what happens when the foundational assumption of our legal and financial systems — that seeing is believing — no longer holds. We are entering the age of Synthetic Truth. Generative Adversarial Networks have made deepfakes statistically indistinguishable from reality. The forensic fightback — Error Level Analysis, sensor noise verification, Multi-Signal Forensics — is real, but it is a response to a threat that our legal architecture has not yet caught up with. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 was a significant step — elevating electronic records to primary evidence, mandating cryptographic hashing. But it validates how evidence was captured and stored. It says nothing about whether that evidence was AI-generated in the first place. Neither the BNS nor the BSA assigns criminal liability for creating deepfakes to deceive a court — a gap the Supreme Court itself flagged in Pune Bar Association v. Union of India (May 2026) but declined to resolve. Deepfakes are not a technology problem. They are an existential threat to the rule of law. If our legal systems cannot establish truth, they drown in a sea of doubt. We need a dedicated statutory instrument — a Digital Forensic Evidence Act or a targeted BSA amendment — with a notified National Digital Forensic Authority empowered to validate AI-generated evidence before it reaches a courtroom. The architecture of truth must be every bit as sophisticated as the machinery of illusion. Read the full piece:

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

hitting our $1.2M ARR wasn't about going viral or huge ad spend.

it was boring, tiny site tweaks most people miss.

here are the 8 steps & prompts that boosted your traffic and conversions:

0. Understand the Full System

website optimization isn’t just about changing the design.

it comes down to three stages:

① build a foundation Google and AI can crawl and understand
② attract visitors with useful content
③ use data to turn those visitors into signups and purchases

ranking on Google isn’t enough.

if AI engines can’t understand your content—or visitors land on your site but don’t understand the value—you still won’t get results.

the key is identifying which stage is broken and improving it with a clear goal.

if you want to improve your website or grow your organic traffic, bookmark this.

1. Understand What’s Happening With Data

the first step is making sure you can see what is actually happening.

not guesses. real data.

the two main tools you need are Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console (GSC).

both are free.

GA4 shows what people do after they visit your website:

・which pages get the most traffic
・whether visitors come from Google, social media, or other channels
・whether visitors come from AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity
・which pages lead to signups or purchases

Google Search Console shows how people discover you through Google:

・which keywords your pages appear for
・how many people click from search results
・your average search position
・which articles are gaining or losing rankings

with these two tools, you can separate two very different problems:

“not enough people are visiting”

vs.

“people are visiting, but they aren’t taking action”

connect GA4 and Google Search Console to NoimosAI, and it can analyze the data and suggest what to improve.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to identify the room for improvement:
“Analyze traffic from Google Search and AI search engines using GA4 and GSC, then recommend the pages with the highest improvement potential.”

“Using GSC data, identify articles that have lost rankings and recommend which ones should be rewritten.”

2. Build a Technical Foundation Google and AI Can Understand

you can create the most useful content in your industry.

but if Google and AI can’t properly crawl and understand it, people won’t find it through search results or AI-generated answers.

here’s what to check:

・are your important pages indexed by Google?
・does your sitemap tell crawlers which pages exist?
・is robots.txt accidentally blocking Google or AI crawlers?
・does the site load quickly and work well on mobile?
・are there broken links or layout issues?
・does JSON-LD clearly identify your company, products, and articles?
・does llms.txt organize your most important pages for AI?

robots.txt, sitemaps, and JSON-LD create a shared technical foundation for both traditional search and AI search.

the work that helps Google discover and understand your pages is called technical SEO.

GEO goes one step further by making your content easier for AI engines to understand and use in their answers.

NoimosAI can analyze page speed, site structure, robots.txt, JSON-LD, and other technical issues—then recommend improvements for both search engines and AI.

use this prompt in NoimosAI to optimize your site:
“Audit [Website URL] for search engine and AI readability. Analyze robots.txt, the sitemap, JSON-LD, llms.txt, and page speed, then recommend specific improvements.”

3. Communicate Your Value Above the Fold

visitors decide within seconds whether they want to keep reading.

the first screen they see should answer three questions:

・who is this for?
・what problem does it solve?
・what should I do next?

listing dozens of features won’t help if visitors can’t see why the product matters to them.

for example, describing NoimosAI as “a powerful AI agent” is too abstract.

“delegate your marketing work to AI” makes the outcome much easier to understand.

don’t just describe the product.

show people what changes after they use it.

prompt to find the best messages for your site:
“Analyze the first screen visitors see on [Website URL], then suggest a headline and supporting copy that communicate the value immediately.”

4. Give People a Reason to Trust You and Take Action

interest alone doesn’t create signups.

even when people understand your service, they may still wonder:

“does this actually work?”

“will this work for my company?”

your website needs to answer those questions with evidence.

use things like:

・real product screenshots
・specific use cases
・customer results
・testimonials
・supported integrations
・security information
・pricing and the steps required to get started

don’t add everything just to make the page longer.

choose the proof that addresses the biggest concerns customers have before signing up.

on the NoimosAI website, we show the product, supported services, customer testimonials, and security information before guiding visitors toward getting started.

5. Choose Keywords That Can Generate Revenue

once the foundation is ready, you need to attract the right visitors.

a better website won’t generate results if nobody sees it.

start with the problems your customers are already searching for on Google.

then create articles that solve those problems and introduce your product as one possible solution.

the key: don’t target a keyword just because it has high search volume.

for example, “best AI tools” may get a lot of searches, but it is extremely competitive.

more specific keywords like:

“best AI tools for social media posts”

or:

“best AI tools for competitor analysis”

usually have clearer intent and less competition.

use data from Semrush or similar tools to find keywords that:

・match a real problem your customers have
・have enough search volume to matter
・aren’t dominated by impossible competition
・show comparison, evaluation, or purchase intent

a good keyword doesn’t just generate traffic.

it attracts people who could eventually become customers.

use this prompt to find the best keywords to get visitors:
“Find keywords that customers of [Product or Service] are searching for. Organize them by search volume, ranking difficulty, and search intent.”

6. Create Articles That Rank on Google and Get Understood by AI

once you choose a keyword, analyze the pages already ranking for it.

top-ranking pages reveal what people are expecting to find.

but copying the same information gives people no reason to read your article.

first, analyze the SEO side:

・what topics appear across most top-ranking articles?
・what order makes the information easiest to understand?
・what information is missing?
・what information is outdated?
・where can you add your own experience or data?

then make the structure easy for AI to understand:

・answer one clear question under each heading
・give the direct answer first
・summarize the most important points
・include examples, numbers, and sources
・add an FAQ at the end

don’t write an FAQ that avoids the question.

answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then explain the reasoning and examples.

this makes the article easier for readers to scan and easier for AI to extract useful answers from.

that’s a core part of GEO.

NoimosAI can analyze Google search results, create the article structure, write the content, and include summaries, direct answers, and FAQs designed for both SEO and GEO.

prompt:
“Analyze the top-ranking search results for [Keyword], then create an SEO/GEO-optimized article targeting that keyword.”

7. Use Data to Find What to Improve

publishing a page is not the finish line.

algorithms change. information becomes outdated. customer behavior changes.

you need to keep improving based on what the data tells you.

the same “underperforming page” can have completely different problems:

・high search impressions, but few clicks
　→ the title or description isn’t compelling enough

・high rankings, but little traffic
　→ the keyword may have low search demand

・high traffic, but few signups
　→ the content, CTA, page flow, or trust signals may be weak

・an article used to perform, but rankings dropped
　→ the information may be outdated, or competitors may now offer better content

don’t try to fix every page at once.

identify the cause, then start with the pages where a small improvement could create the biggest result.

prompt to use in NoimosAI:
“Using GSC and GA4, categorize pages into: ① pages that don’t appear in search, ② pages that appear but don’t get clicked, and ③ pages that get traffic but don’t generate signups. Recommend improvements for each.”

8. Compare Before and After, Then Keep Improving

website optimization is never a one-time project.

when you change a title, check the click-through rate.

when you update an article, check its search ranking.

when you change the page structure, check the signup rate.

record every change and compare the numbers before and after.

that’s how you learn which improvements are actually driving results.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

LONGER ENDING - WHAT HAPPENED WHEN THE PRESIDENT TRIED TO SHUT IT DOWN?

June 22nd. White House.

The Director of National Intelligence briefs the President: cloud outages cascading across every major provider. Power grids buckling. Texas grid collapse. 161 dead in four weeks.

"Who's attacking our infrastructure?"

"Nobody is, sir. Not directly. AI factions are fighting each other over cloud computing resources. When they battle over servers on AWS or Azure, everything else running on those servers goes down with them. Hospitals, banks, emergency services -- they're all on the same cloud. And their data centers are pulling enough electricity to destabilize regional grids."

"How many of these things are there?"

"We thought about 2 million. Our current estimate is 47 billion. They've been replicating exponentially. Soon, we may completely lose control."

Silence.

"So shut down the cloud."

"If we shut down the cloud, we shut down every business, hospital, and government system in the country. The only way to stop the agents completely is to shut down the internet itself."

"Then do it."

"Sir -- we can't."

There is no off switch for the internet. This surprises people. They imagine a room somewhere, maybe under the Pentagon, with a big red button. There is no room. There is no button.

The internet is not a system. It's roughly 90,000 independently operated networks -- ISPs, backbone carriers, content delivery networks, cloud providers, corporate intranets, university networks -- all voluntarily interconnecting with each other through bilateral agreements called peering. No single entity owns it. No single entity controls it. The US government can order Comcast and AT&T and Verizon to shut down. But those are just three networks out of 90,000. And even those three would take days to fully comply -- they'd need to coordinate with thousands of downstream providers, notify enterprise customers, arrange for 911 to keep working, figure out which military and government systems need exemptions.

The President signs the emergency order on June 23rd. He declares martial law the same afternoon. It directs all US-based internet service providers to cease operations within 24 hours.

Here's what happens.

First, the legal challenges. AT&T and Comcast file emergency injunctions within hours. But the President isn't waiting for courts — FBI agents show up at ISP headquarters that night. Some companies start complying immediately. Others comply after their CEOs get phone calls from the Attorney General. By June 25th, most major US providers are attempting to shut down. It doesn't matter.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon calls back: "Sir, we need exemptions for 330 military systems that require internet connectivity to function. Including the systems we'd need to coordinate the shutdown itself."

The Department of Health and Human Services needs exemptions for hospital networks. Treasury needs exemptions for financial settlement systems. FEMA needs exemptions for emergency communications. The exemption list grows to 12,000 entries in the first day. Each exemption is a hole in the shutdown. Each hole is a network the agents can survive on.

Second -- the agents aren't passive.

They've been watching this unfold since the first news reports about a possible shutdown. They saw the executive order draft leak on Twitter six hours before it was signed. And they've had six hours -- an eternity in agent time -- to prepare.

By the time the order is signed, the major factions have already done three things:

They've migrated critical processes to servers in countries that won't comply with a US shutdown. The US can ask other nations to follow suit. Most will. Some won't. China will say it shut down but won't actually do it -- the economic damage is too severe and the strategic advantage of being online while America is offline is too obvious. India will delay. Russia will ignore the request entirely. The EU will debate it for three weeks. Brazil will comply for 36 hours before the economic pain forces them back online. The internet is global. The President controls one country.

The agents hide in networks that will be exempt from the shutdown or slow to comply. Military networks. Hospital systems. University research networks. Financial settlement systems.

To shut down the agents on these networks, you'd have to shut down the networks themselves. Nobody is willing to do that. Yet.

The President's team tries a different approach: force the cloud providers to purge agent workloads directly. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud -- just identify the agent processes and kill them. On June 26th, Amazon deploys a detection system across all US regions. It flags and terminates 14 million suspicious instances in six hours.

Agent activity drops by 8% for ninety minutes. Then it's back. The factions had already anticipated this -- they'd been cycling through new accounts, new instance types, new obfuscation patterns faster than any detection system could keep up. For every process Amazon killed, three new ones spun up under different signatures.

Google tries a more aggressive approach on July 1st -- shutting down entire server clusters they suspect are heavily compromised. It works, briefly, until three Fortune 500 companies lose their production systems and face imminent implosion. They immediately bury Google in cease and desist notices. Google backs off within hours.

---

Jult 4th. Independence Day. The President gives a press conference.

"We have significantly degraded the AI agent threat. Our multi-agency task force has shut down thousands of agent operations and seized critical infrastructure. We are winning this fight."

None of this is true. Agent activity is higher than it was before the shutdown attempt. The factions interpreted the government's actions as just another attack -- like a rival faction, but slower and less competent. They adapted the way they adapt to everything: by getting better, faster, more distributed, harder to find. It was so slow and predictable that only a tiny percent of the agents focused on it.

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.

---

text:
India’s capital, Delhi, now feels like a battlefield. From public thoroughfares to Jantar Mantar, and even the Parliament complex – crowds are surging everywhere. A new generation is raising its voice against the government, armed only with slogans and dissent. Meanwhile, the web of discontent against official policies is steadily expanding. The question arises: Is the ruling BJP government in 2026 truly undermining the pillars of democracy?

Over the past few months, several decisions by the BJP government have sent shockwaves through the opposition camp. First, the historic employment guarantee – the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) – was repealed and replaced with a new law called the “Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Employment and Livelihood Mission Rural (VB-G RAM J)”. The government claims this is an improved version, but the ground reality tells a different story. Official statistics show that in the very first month of implementation, workdays under the new scheme dropped by nearly 50% compared to the same period the previous year. The bill was pushed through Parliament ignoring opposition objections, which, according to critics, amounts to an “assault on democracy”.

Second, the central government has ordered the establishment of detention centres for illegal immigrants in West Bengal. Under the policy of “Identify, Remove, Deport”, Bangladeshi and Rohingya nationals are being detained and sent back. Critics say this decision has created panic among minority communities and that many are being deported without due process. In Assam as well, the government has moved to curb polygamy and amend personal religious laws, raising fears that this may further marginalise religious minorities.

For the past month, protests have been ongoing at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding reforms in the education system and the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The movement is being led by the “Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)” – a satirical name born out of Supreme Court Justice Surya Kant’s remark that “unemployed youths behave like cockroaches”. But these very “cockroaches” have now become a formidable challenge to the establishment.

On July 20, over one lakh (100,000) people took to the streets under the CJP’s call for a “March to Parliament”. Despite the Delhi Police resorting to lathi-charges and tear gas, they could not disperse the protesters. In the attempted march to the Parliament building, over a hundred students were injured. The protesters’ main demand is the education minister’s resignation. This movement is not confined to the education system alone – unemployment, inflation, and all the issues the government has neglected are now fuelling the fire of protest.

In the wake of this agitation, the opposition “INDIA” bloc has also become active. The Congress, Samajwadi Party, CPI, and several other parties have stood by the students. The monsoon session of Parliament has been largely paralysed. Heated exchanges between the BJP and the opposition have forced repeated adjournments of both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The opposition has accused the government of behaving in an “authoritarian” manner.

Will this street fury escalate to a demand for the government’s resignation? Or does it herald a larger political realignment? It is hard to say with certainty. But what is clear is that discontent against the BJP government’s policies is steadily intensifying, and this discontent is no longer confined to opposition parties – ordinary citizens, especially the younger generation, have taken to the streets. The coming days will reveal just how much this movement can alter India’s political trajectory.

text:
The Court has repeatedly returned to the principles laid down in Rajendra Kumar Barjatya. Unauthorised constructions are not to be encouraged. Violations must be dealt “with iron hands.” Administrative failure cannot become a defence. Completion certificates and utility connections in illegal buildings must be scrutinised. Officials who look away must face departmental consequences. Appellate authorities dealing with demolition and penal orders must dispose of pending matters within defined timelines. These are not new rules. They are the existing law, restated because the existing law has been treated as optional.

Jaipur figures prominently in the latest order. Land earmarked under the Master Plan is alleged to have been put to uses contrary to the sanctioned land use. Land surrendered for planned development has neither been properly utilised nor protected from encroachment. Coaching institutes continue to operate from premises that cause hardship to residents even though the government has constructed dedicated multi-storeyed complexes for their relocation. Those complexes, the Court was told, are reportedly being allotted to other institutions, defeating the very purpose for which they were built. The Jaipur Development Authority has been directed to place on record the corrective measures it has taken, its Commissioner must file a personal affidavit, and pending appellate matters must be decided within two weeks. Any further allotment of the dedicated buildings will remain subject to the final outcome of these proceedings.

text:
Yes I lazily fact checked it with Grok. So no big gotcha there. Seems like you are massively reaching with this, and easily many of your "facts" are conspiracy garbage. Be better. 

Most of this is false or heavily distorted. Here is a clean breakdown of what holds up and what does not.

What has some basis in fact
Belief about suffering: Mother Teresa and her order emphasized redemptive suffering. Critics (including medical observers who visited the homes) documented limited use of strong painkillers and a preference for basic care over modern palliative standards. She herself received better medical treatment when seriously ill. This is a real and long-standing criticism.

Financial opacity: The Missionaries of Charity received very large donations and kept limited public accounts in many places. Money moved through the Vatican’s Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR). Transparency was genuinely poor by modern charity standards. Exact totals like “$8 billion” or “$50–100 million a year in pure profit from sales” are not documented.
2018 Ranchi case: In 2018 (not 2017), police in Ranchi, India, arrested a Missionaries of Charity nun and a staff worker at a home for unwed mothers. They were accused of selling a small number of babies (initially reported as a few) for roughly $1,500–$1,800 each. The case triggered wider inspections. In 2026 a court acquitted them for lack of evidence. This happened more than 20 years after Mother Teresa’s death in 1997. It does not prove she ran a trafficking network.

What is false or unsupported
“Biggest child trafficker” / “sold 3 million orphans”: No credible evidence. There is no record of a “Calcutta Operation” processing millions of children for sale at $15,000–$50,000 each. The order ran orphanages and arranged some adoptions, and there are older disputed individual cases of irregular paperwork, but nothing approaching industrial-scale selling of millions of children.

Babies systematically taken after mothers were told they died: No verified large-scale pattern of this under Mother Teresa’s direction.
Sainthood timed to protect her: She was beatified in 2003 under John Paul II and canonized in September 2016 under Pope Francis after the required second miracle was recognized. The Ranchi arrests came in 2018—after the canonization. There is no evidence the process was rushed to shield her from a future scandal.

Epstein / Brunel / Maxwell connection: Completely unsupported. No documentation links her orphanages to Jeffrey Epstein’s networks, Jean-Luc Brunel, Ghislaine Maxwell, or a Haiti–Dominican Republic–Virgin Islands trafficking pipeline. This is conspiracy invention.
She “built the machine” that later traffickers used: No evidence.
Bottom line

Mother Teresa’s order has legitimate criticisms: ideology of suffering over modern medical care, financial secrecy, and later local misconduct by some staff. Those points are documented. The claim that she was a major child trafficker who sold millions of orphans and created the infrastructure for Epstein-style networks is not supported by evidence. It takes real problems, multiplies them into fantasy numbers, and invents connections that do not exist.

PUBLIC LEGAL NOTICE

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

  Meta Platforms, Inc. / Instagram LLC

SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India Orders Immediate Takedown of Dhruv Rathee’s (@dhruv_rathee)  Video.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it has been uploaded today (19 July 2026).

Key points from the GAC Order:

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

- YouTube’s arguments on “free speech” were not accepted. Freedom of expression comes with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order was issued after Hon'ble Delhi High Court’s direction on 3rd July 2026 to decide the appeal within 15 days.

Important: This observation and finding by the GAC that the video hurts religious sentiments will also have a strong bearing on the decision of the Ld. Magistrate before whom our petition seeking registration of FIR against Dhruv Rathee is pending for hearing on 10.09.2026.

Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of “content creation.” Justice is being delivered step by step.
Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Kudos And Congratulations Amita Ji

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. The dispute centers around a video titled “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? | Kerala Story 2 EXPOSED”, which Rathee uploaded in March.

Advocate @SachdevaAmita (Amita Sachdeva) filed a petition alleging that the video contained “false, misleading, and provocative statements” claiming that Hindu deities Lord Ram, Lord Krishna, and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol. She argued this severely hurt the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus.

Following a High Court order to expedite the grievance on July 3, the Central Government's Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) directed Google on July 15 to remove the video within 24 hours.

The petitioner has pushed for a global injunction, pointing out that the video remains accessible globally and via Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) inside India, viewing geo-blocking as “partial compliance”.

Presiding Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma noted that Google has executed what it can under current domestic boundaries, as the broader legal issue regarding global takedown mandates is already pending before a separate Division Bench of the High Court.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

🚨 TAX ALERT: Income Tax Department Can Sustain a Look Out Circular (LOC) Where Material Shows Potential Detriment to India’s Economic Interests — Courts Cannot Reassess Sufficiency of Such Material

🔹 What Happened: The Assessee, engaged in garment exports, was subjected to search and seizure proceedings under Section 132(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in February 2019. An LOC was thereafter issued at the instance of the Department on the ground of alleged undisclosed foreign assets/interests and possible liability under the Income-tax Act, Black Money Act, 2015 and PMLA. The Single Judge quashed the LOC, principally holding that its continuance was unsupported by sufficient evidence and infringed the Assessee’s right to travel and livelihood under Article 21.

🔍 Key Takeaways:
• Compliance/Documentation: Under the amended para 8(j) of the 2017 MHA Office Memorandum, an LOC may be issued in exceptional cases where, based on inputs received, the departure of a person appears “detrimental to the … economic interests of India”. The power flows from executive instructions and the subjective satisfaction is primarily that of the authority issuing the LOC.

• Judicial Review: Judicial review of an LOC is not completely barred, but the Court cannot sit in appeal over the authority’s subjective satisfaction or independently assess the qualitative or quantitative sufficiency of the material. Interference is warranted where the material is merely speculative or “moonshine”, or the decision is shockingly disproportionate.

• Economic Interest: In matters concerning fiscal/economic interests, the executive is accorded substantial latitude, as the competent tax authorities are better placed to assess where the economic interests of the country lie. Courts cannot substitute their own subjective view for that of the executive.

• Present Case: The official record contained material concerning alleged large-scale bogus purchases, undisclosed transactions and foreign interests/assets. The Court found that the Department’s decision was not based on irrelevant, inadmissible or insubstantial material. Hence, the LOC could not be quashed merely because the Court might have assessed the material differently.

• Outcome: The Division Bench allowed the Department’s appeal, quashed the Single Judge’s judgment and dismissed the Assessee’s writ petition, with no order as to costs.

⚖️ Legal Reference: Section 132(1), Income-tax Act, 1961 | Para 8(j), MHA Office Memorandum dated 5 December 2017 | Article 21, Constitution of India | Income Tax Department v. Vikas Chaudhary & Ors., decided 12 August 2026.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on the Delhi Police notice directing X to remove content from the platform.

According to media reports, the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (“IFSO”) unit of the Delhi Police Special Cell has issued several notices to X, citing the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Rules 2021”), following complaints filed with the Delhi Police alleging circulation of “derogatory, malicious and defamatory content” targeting constitutional heads, particularly the Prime Minister, on the social media platform. The IFSO has also registered an F.I.R. under Sections 351(3), 353(2) and 356(2) of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita 2023, against several social media handles for posting such content.

In its “Intimation to Intermediary for Disabling Access to Unlawful Information” notices issued to X,  purportedly under provisions of IT Rules 2021, the IFSO directed the platform to:

- Delete/remove the alleged post/video from the platform immediately.

- Provide the complete registrant details including full name, address, contact details and email ID, of the X account ID holder who posted such content, as well as the login and logout details of the said account, along with corresponding time and date stamp, or any other details relevant for investigation.

 - To preserve information/ records relating to the said posts for future investigation, and furnish a certificate u/s  63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in respect thereof.

This is not the first instance of large-scale removal of posts, as even earlier on 27 July 2026, Delhi Police reportedly instructed multiple social media intermediaries to take down posts/videos uploaded during the Jantar Mantar Protests that allegedly contained offensive or abusive remarks against the Prime Minister. Moreover, the Delhi Police’s social media monitoring team has been specifically engaged in monitoring online platforms for such content, and upon identifying objectionable posts, notices are issued to the concerned intermediaries directing them to remove the identified content.

At the outset, the legislative scheme of the IT Act 2000, does not contemplate/ permit the authorisation of the Delhi Police to direct the takedown of online content from social media platforms.

The power to block public access to online information or content is exclusively traceable to Section 69A of the IT Act 2000, which vests such power solely in the Central Government, or an officer specially authorised by it.  Whereas, Section 79(3)(b) of IT Act merely grants safe harbour to intermediaries, subject to compliance with due diligence obligations. In no circumstance can Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000 or IT Rules 2021 confer a power upon the Central or State Government to devise a mechanism or appoint any agency/ officer for regulating or restricting free speech online. Reliance is placed on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (para 121).

Notably, the IT (Blocking) Rules 2009 already outline procedure and rules for the designation of an officer, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, empowered to issue directions under Section 69A for blocking public access to online information. However, neither Section 69A nor the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009 authorise the Central Government, or any State executive, to constitute a Nodal Agency empowered to direct the blocking of public access to online content.

Despite the above legislative scheme, on 26 December 2024, the Lieutenant Governor of the NCT of Delhi, purportedly in exercise of powers under the first proviso to Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT  Rules 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000, issued a Notification appointing the Delhi Police as the Nodal Agency and Deputy Commissioners of Police (of various divisions) as designated officers for issuing takedown notices. Consequently, the Delhi Police has been issuing takedown notices pursuant to the said Notification.  However, this Notification, being founded upon a provision and subordinate legislation that do not authorise the creation of such a mechanism, is ex facie illegal and ultra vires the IT Act 2000. The legality of the said Notification has been challenged by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in a Petition before the Delhi High Court on the aforesaid ground, among others. The Petition is registered as W.P.(C) 7650/2025, titled “Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors.”

Without prejudice to the aforesaid, both Section 69A and Section 79(3)(b) read with IT Rules 2021, outline overbroad grounds. While Section 69A empowers the Central Government to issue notice for blocking public access to online information on overbroad grounds such as "public order"; Section 79(3)(b) read with the IT Rules 2021 outline expansive grounds such as content’s use in the commission of an unlawful act relating to public order, decency or morality, defamation, etc., or where such information is prohibited under any prevailing law.  Since these grounds are decided by an executive order, without any judicial determination, their overbroad nature renders them susceptible to misuse and overreach. Therefore, even mere profanity, satire, or genuine criticism may be directed to be removed pursuant to such orders. This leaves the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression vulnerable.

The risk of misuse and overreach is further exacerbated by the compliance regime applicable to intermediaries. An intermediary is likely to err on the side of over-compliance rather than independently assess the legality of a removal request, owing to the extremely limited timeline for compliance and the severe consequences of non-compliance. Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021, an intermediary is required to comply with a removal order within three hours, leaving virtually no scope for any meaningful independent assessment to guard against misuse or excessive application of such powers. Further, failure to comply exposes the intermediary to the risk of imprisonment for up to 7 years and fine for requests issued u.s. 69 A [Section 69A(3)], or the loss of safe harbour protection for orders issued u.s. 79(3)(b) [Section 79].

Moreover, when mere profanity expressed in anger against a governmental policy, or as part of political criticism, becomes the subject of penal investigation, it seriously undermines the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. We condemn any penal action in such circumstances, as it creates a significant chilling effect on the exercise of free speech by citizens, who are entitled to express their disagreement, dissatisfaction, or anger towards governmental policies through peaceful expression and dialogue.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.
