Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

To safeguard the online freedom of speech of these users, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s RightsLine provides free legal assistance and support to anyone facing content takedowns or account suspensions. Our team can help individuals understand their options and navigate the available redress mechanisms.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed directions to block online content were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, according to data accessed by The Indian Express. That means roughly one blocking order every 68 seconds, or about 1,275 a day.

The surge came during a period that also saw student protests against exam leaks at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, which began in early June and ended on July 25.

Instagram received the largest share, with around 1 lakh orders, followed by Facebook with about 80,000 and YouTube with nearly 15,000. A single order can cover hundreds of posts or accounts.

Most of the directions were issued by central and state government agencies, with a large number sent through the Home Ministry’s Sahyog portal. For comparison, RTI records accessed by The Indian Express showed that just 2,312 blocking orders were sent to 19 online platforms through Sahyog between October 2024 and October 2025, an average of about six a day.

The report also found that Meta has connected its systems to the Sahyog portal to meet the government’s tighter 2 to 3-hour deadline for removing flagged content. This allows directions uploaded through the system to be acted on automatically, without a separate human review by Meta, according to the report.

The scale of the increase, and the use of automated takedowns, puts a sharper focus on how India regulates content online and how platforms respond to government directions.

Most "AI sales automation" posts show:

Lead → GPT → Email

That's not an operating system. That's a demo.

A real system has to:

Here's the full build. (1/3)
—
STEP 1 — DEFINE THE SYSTEM
The objective: turn a raw lead into a verified, human-approved sales action.
The system should be able to answer: Who is this company? Are they a fit? Why might they care now? Who owns the problem? What evidence supports that? What should we say? Is it factually safe? Should a human approve it? What happened afterward?
Build it as a state machine. Every lead has a state — and the workflow decides the state, never the AI.
Success path: NEW → ENRICHING → RESEARCHING → SCORED → PERSONALIZING → VERIFYING → PENDING_APPROVAL → APPROVED → SENT → REPLIED
Failure states: DUPLICATE, INVALID, RESEARCH_FAILED, VERIFICATION_FAILED, HUMAN_REVIEW, SUPPRESSED, SEND_FAILED

STEP 2 — THE ARCHITECTURE
[see image 1]
Lead Source → Normalization → Deduplication → Enrichment → Research → ICP + Intent + Buyer → Context Packet → Personalization → Fact Verifier → Human Approval → Send Gate → Email + CRM → Reply Classifier → Sales / Nurture / Suppress / Human
Build this as 8 separate n8n workflows, not one giant 100-node canvas:
01_lead_intake 02_research_and_scoring 03_personalization_and_verification 04_human_approval 05_send_gate 06_reply_handler 07_error_handler 08_monitoring

n8n → orchestration PostgreSQL → state + audit history LLM → reasoning and structured generation Search/enrichment provider → external company/contact data CRM → system of record Email provider → outbound/inbound Slack → human approval
Credential rule: never put secrets inside code nodes, prompts, database records, Slack messages, or lead JSON. Use n8n's credential store / environment config only. The AI sees business data. It never sees credentials.

The AI recommends. Rules validate. Humans authorize sensitive actions.

Always: AI → VALIDATE → VERIFY → HUMAN → SEND

[see image 2]

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;

CREATE TABLE leads ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), company_name TEXT NOT NULL, domain TEXT, contact_name TEXT, contact_title TEXT, email TEXT, source TEXT, status TEXT DEFAULT 'NEW', icp_score NUMERIC, intent_score NUMERIC, confidence NUMERIC, created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(), updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW() );

CREATE INDEX idx_leads_email ON leads (LOWER(email)); CREATE INDEX idx_leads_domain ON leads (LOWER(domain)); CREATE INDEX idx_leads_status ON leads (status); CREATE INDEX idx_leads_icp_score ON leads (icp_score);

Without indexes, duplicate checks and queue queries get expensive as the table grows.

Five more tables round out the schema:

research — raw structured research + evidence + sources (never store just the summary, you need the evidence later)
messages — subject/body, personalization_reason, verification_status, approval_status, human_edited_body
lead_events — the audit log: lead_id, event_type, agent, input, output, confidence, timestamp
suppressions — email/domain/reason, checked before every send
lead_state_history — previous_state, new_state, reason, timestamp for every transition
Each gets its own indexes on lead_id and the fields you'll filter on (approval_status, verification_status, email, domain).
—
STEP 6 — DEFINE THE ICP BEFORE TOUCHING AI

Don't tell the model "find good leads." Give it measurable criteria as one canonical config object, reused across every agent:

{ "industries": ["B2B SaaS", "FinTech", "Professional Services"], "employee_min": 50, "employee_max": 500, "regions": ["United States", "Canada", "United Kingdom"], "target_roles": ["CEO", "Founder", "VP Sales", "Head of Growth"], "minimum_score": 70 }

Pass this same object into the ICP scorer, the buyer mapper, the research agent, and the personalization agent. Change the ICP once — not four prompts.
—
STEP 7 — THE SCORING MODEL
Industry fit — 20 Company size — 20 Role fit — 20 Problem fit — 20 Geography — 10 Business signal — 10 TOTAL — 100
Each category must return a structured object, never a bare number:
{ "score": 0, "max": 20, "reason": "", "evidence": [] }
Never let the model just return "87." You need to know why it returned 87 — and the total should be calculated deterministically in code, not by the LLM.

Routing (numeric, never natural language like "good lead"):

85–100 → PRIORITY 70–84 → DEEPER RESEARCH 50–69 → NURTURE 0–49 → STOP

That's the foundation: architecture, stack, database, and scoring model.

Part 2 covers lead intake, enrichment, research, the verification loop, and how the writer and the fact-checker are forced to see the exact same evidence. →

AI Sales Operating System — Part 2/3

Part 1 covered the architecture, database, and scoring model. Now: how a raw lead actually becomes verified, evidence-backed research — and why the writer and the fact-checker must see the exact same data. (2/3)

—

STEP 8 — LEAD INTAKE

n8n Webhook, POST /sales/lead, respond immediately.

Test payload:

{ "company_name": "Example Inc", "website": "https://t.co/ALNMupgMwp", "contact_name": "Jane Doe", "contact_title": "VP Sales", "email": "jane@example.com", "source": "manual_test" }
Don't connect expensive enrichment nodes until the raw webhook payload is stable.
—
STEP 9 — NORMALIZE BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE
Domain: strip protocol, strip "www.", lowercase. https://t.co/bU31yw7Cm3 → https://t.co/urMSOrwWa1
Email: trim + lowercase, then validate format. Jane@Example.com → jane@example.com
const valid = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+.[^\s@]+$/.test(email);
If invalid → status INVALID → stop. Don't let a malformed lead enter the pipeline.

—

STEP 10 — DUPLICATE CHECK

This is the query that's usually wrong in copy-pasted tutorials — make sure the parameters are properly separated:

SELECT id, status FROM leads WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER($1) OR LOWER(domain) = LOWER($2) LIMIT 1;
Params: $1 = normalized_email, $2 = normalized_domain.

Match found → DUPLICATE, log event, stop. No match → create the lead with status 'NEW', save the returned UUID, and carry lead_id through every downstream node.
Debugging duplicates that slip through? Check in this order: email normalization, domain normalization, SQL parameter binding, database connection, then the actual duplicate record. Also check case sensitivity, trailing spaces, the "www." prefix, protocol, and subdomain handling — that's where most false negatives hide.

—
STEP 11 — PROVIDER ABSTRACTION (do this before calling any external API)
Every provider — enrichment, CRM, email — gets normalized to your own internal schema immediately after the response comes back. Example, enrichment:
External response: { "company": { "name": "...", "employees": 180, "industry": "B2B SaaS" } }
Converted immediately to: { "company_name": "...", "employee_count": 180, "industry": "B2B SaaS" }

const company = https://t.co/sY4ulovjbI || {}; return { json: { company_name: https://t.co/GOVjMSPq1j ?? null, employee_count: company.employees ?? null, industry: company.industry ?? null } };

If the provider changes its response format, only this adapter changes — nothing downstream. This is the difference between a system you can swap providers on in an afternoon, and one you have to rebuild.

Required enrichment fields before continuing: company_name, domain, industry, company_size, country. Missing any of them → RETRY once → still missing → HUMAN_REVIEW. Never silently continue with incomplete data.

—

STEP 12 — RESEARCH: FACTS, NOT A SALES PITCH
System prompt:
"You are a B2B company research analyst. Your ONLY responsibility is factual research. Do not write sales messages. Do not recommend products. Do not invent information."
Required output:
{ "company_name": "", "industry": "", "business_model": "", "employee_range": "", "core_product": "", "target_customer": "", "growth_signals": [], "hiring_signals": [], "expansion_signals": [], "relevant_business_problem": "", "evidence": [], "sources": [], "confidence": 0.0 }

Hard rules: every material claim requires evidence. If evidence is unavailable, return UNKNOWN. Never turn an assumption into a fact. Never manufacture a buying signal. Never fabricate a source. Never write outreach. JSON only.

Each evidence item is structured, not a loose sentence:
{ "claim": "...", "source": "...", "evidence": "...", "confidence": 0.0 }

That structure is what makes verification possible later. A claim with no evidence cannot be used for personalization — full stop.

Validate the model's JSON before trusting it: is it parseable, are required keys present, are arrays actually arrays, is confidence numeric, does evidence actually contain sources? Malformed → retry once → retry again → fail → human review. Log the raw model response separately from the parsed one; never overwrite the original failure.

—

STEP 13 — SCORE, DETECT INTENT, MAP THE BUYER

[see image 3]
ICP Scorer input: company + contact + research + your ICP config. Output mirrors the scoring model from Part 1, with every sub-score capped (industry_fit ≤ 20, size_fit ≤ 20, etc.) and the total calculated deterministically in code — never by the LLM.

Intent detection looks for: new hiring, leadership change, expansion, new product, new market, tech change, strategic or operational initiatives. A verified announcement outweighs a vague inference. If nothing credible exists, the output is explicitly NO_CURRENT_SIGNAL — never manufacture urgency.
Buyer mapping identifies the role most likely to own the problem, prioritizing: problem ownership → decision influence → budget authority → operational responsibility. The system can infer "VP Sales" from verified org context. It must never invent "Jane Doe is definitely the buyer" unless that identity is actually verified — if not, return ROLE_ONLY.

—
STEP 14 — ONE CONTEXT PACKET, NOT THREE VERSIONS OF THE TRUTH
{ "lead": {}, "company": {}, "contact": {}, "icp": {}, "intent": {}, "buyer": {}, "evidence": [], "unknowns": [], "confidence": 0.0 }
Store it in its own table, keyed by lead_id. Without a controlled packet, the research agent, the writer, and the verifier can each end up working off a different version of "what's true." With one packet, the writer and the verifier are guaranteed to see identical facts — which is the only way verification means anything.
—
STEP 15 — PERSONALIZATION, WITH HARD LIMITS
Structure: observed change → why it may create a relevant problem → specific value → simple next step. Never generic praise ("I was impressed by your amazing company...").
Writer rules: use only facts in the context packet. Never invent familiarity, company activity, pain points, or results. Never make unapproved promises. If confidence is below 0.80, return HUMAN_REVIEW_REQUIRED instead of a message.
Output: { "subject": "", "body": "", "personalization_reason": "", "evidence_used": [], "confidence": 0.0 }

Set explicit limits on subject length, body length, number of claims, number of personalization facts, and CTA count — otherwise the model will happily turn a two-line email into an essay.

—

STEP 16 — THE FACT VERIFIER LOOP

This is the gate that actually earns the word "verified" in your marketing copy.

Verifier checks the generated message against the research evidence for: company facts, person facts, timing, personalization claims, promises, and unsupported assumptions.

{ "decision": "PASS", "errors": [], "required_changes": [], "verified_claims": [], "unsupported_claims": [], "confidence": 0.0 }

PASS only when every material factual claim is supported by supplied evidence. The verifier never infers missing evidence to fill a gap.

Routing: PASS → approval. FAIL → rewrite → re-verify. Cap it at 2 attempts total — after that, HUMAN_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Never build an unlimited AI retry loop; increment verification_attempts on every pass through.
Confidence gates, layered on top (not instead of) hard validation: 0.90+ → normal continuation 0.75–0.89 → continue, but flag <0.75 → human review
Confidence is a signal, not permission. The workflow still enforces the hard checks regardless of what the score says.
That's the reasoning pipeline — research, scoring, intent, buyer mapping, personalization, and verification, all forced through one shared, evidence-backed context.
Part 3: the human approval gate, the send gate that blocks anything unapproved, suppression and rate limiting, reply handling, and how one lead moves start-to-finish through the whole system. →

Alright, since the Dunning-Kruger Awards this week are going to people who apparently cannot tell the difference between one tragic murder case and an entire population, if we’re gonna go there, let’s go there.

I got these statistics from Grok regarding postpartum issues and murder rates. Feel free to fact-check.

I asked Grok:

What percent of American men commit murder?
• Roughly 0.3–0.7%. That’s 3 to 7 out of every thousand men, or around 1 in 150–300.

What percent of American women commit murder?
• Roughly 0.04–0.1%. That’s 4 to 10 out of every ten thousand women, or around 1 in 1,000–2,500.

Women account for only about 10–12% of known murder offenders. Men make up the rest.

In contrast, the lifetime murder victimization rate is 0.68% for males and 0.19% for females. Compare these to the numbers above. While men are at higher odds of being murdered, men’s average population risks of murdering versus being murdered are similar. Women, however, are at much greater risk of being murdered than of committing murder.

Now let’s look at postpartum moms.

10–15% of mothers will experience postpartum depression (PPD). Only 0.1–0.2% of mothers will experience postpartum psychosis (PPP). PPD is 50 to 100 times more common than PPP.

The total rate of filicide by postpartum women is extremely rare—on the order of a few cases per 100,000 (well under 0.01%, and typically estimated in the range of roughly 2–8 per 100,000 live births for maternal involvement in infant homicide, depending on the exact definition and data source).

Postpartum psychosis (distinct from the more common postpartum depression or “baby blues”) occurs in roughly 1–2 per 1,000 births. Older estimates sometimes cited an ~4% risk of infanticide among untreated cases, but this figure has been questioned as potentially overstated based on misreadings of follow-up studies. The absolute contribution to overall numbers remains tiny.

How do these numbers compare?

The number of postpartum women who commit filicide is much smaller than the number of women who commit any kind of murder, which is itself much smaller than the number of men who commit murder.

10–15% of mothers will experience postpartum depression.

Only 0.1–0.2% of women will experience postpartum psychosis specifically (1–2 out of every 1,000 births). This is lower than the percentage of men who murder (3 to 7 out of every 1,000 men).

Read that again. Postpartum psychosis—without even factoring in murder—is less common than men who murder.

Of those with untreated postpartum psychosis, as many as 4 out of every 100 may commit murder, but those numbers are in question and may be lower. Since postpartum psychosis is itself rate, we are looking at up to four percent of 0.1–0.2% is 0.004%, or four out of every hundred thousand. The smallest number we've seen here.

So: out of every hundred thousand births, up to four may result in a postpartum-psychosis-related murder. This is roughly on par with the number of men who kill their own children — a few per hundred thousand. Meanwhile, the number of men who murder anyone is about 75 to 175 times higher than the number of women who kill their children.

If people are going to get hysterical about this issue—senselessly equating postpartum women with postpartum depression, postpartum depression with postpartum psychosis, and postpartum psychosis with murder—then by the same logic we should equate men in general with murder, because the percent of men who murder is higher than the percent of women with any of these issues.

Thankfully, I’m afflicted by no such hysteria. I’m happily married, get along well with many good men, and can tell the difference between a normal, decent man and an internet troll with no greater purpose in life than harassing women online between porn sessions. Grow up and get a life, fellas.

text:
Today (24th October2025), when I read @pbmehta
Sir's article in @IndianExpress
(THE COLLAPSE OF SINCERITY) , it reminded me of another closely related article of @_YogendraYadav sir (THE NATIONALISM WE FORGOT) that also appeared in same newspaper in May 2025. I am not saying that their arguments are absolutely wrong, what i am trying is to give balanced counter arguments 

🔥Noise ≠ nihilism; patriotism ≠ persecution. India’s constitutional engine still forges truthful speech + plural nation—by design, doctrine, and delivery. Watch the evidence. #UPSC #GS2 #GS4 #PSIR ⚖️🇮🇳

A. “Collapse of sincerity” vs “Working constitutional speech-market” — juxtaposed refutation

Claim (Mehta): algorithms monetise performance; sincerity is dead.

Counter (law-anchored): India’s system builds, protects, and disciplines truthful communication.

Free speech spine intact: Art.19(1)(a); limits only under Art.19(2)—sovereignty, integrity (via 16th Amend., 1963), public order, decency, contempt, defamation, incitement.

Shreya Singhal (2015): struck 66A IT Act; mandated narrow tests (“incitement”, “tendency to create”). Sincerity space preserved.

Right to know fuels deliberation: PUCL v. Union (2003) & ADR (2002)—candidate disclosures as Art.19(1)(a); RTI Act 2005 operationalises truth access, not performance.

State coercion checked: Anuradha Bhasin (2020)—internet restrictions must be proportional, reasoned, reviewable. Kaushal Kishor (2023)—remedies exist for ministerial speech harm; no blanket gag on political speech.

Harmful speech contained, not chilled: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation to protect Art.21 reputation; Amish Devgan (2020) clarified hate-speech thresholds—ethics by law, not by vibe.

Platform due-diligence (not censorship): IT (Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021—grievance officers, 36-hr takedown on court/LEA orders, traceability for heinous crimes; 69A IT Act blocking only via speaking orders + review (per Shreya Singhal).

Election truth-checks: Model Code of Conduct, cVIGIL, paid-news rules; ECI + SVEEP strengthen voter information.

Civic transparency expanding: Open Government Data, Proactive RTI (s.4), Social Audit (MNREGA/SSA rules)—institutionalise fact visibility.

Bottom line: The architecture prizes sincerity by rights (19(1)(a)), guardrails (19(2)), remedies (courts/RTI/ECI). The market is noisy; the constitution makes it corrigible.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

In 2024 December, Indian security forces recovered a Starlink antenna/router alongside weapons from militants in northeast India.

The markings on the device indicated that they were brought in from Myanmar across the border.

Reports also indicated that a lot of these devices had been smuggled across the border. Internet signals were spilling over from Myanmar, and bad actors used them to bypass prolonged internet shutdowns during times of unrest.

Allowing internet infrastructure to be operated from outside the country makes it difficult for the government to effectively implement law-and-order measures in critical areas.

This has recently happened in many parts of the world, including Iran, according to news reports. This is what worries the Indian security agencies.

Satellite internet is not limited by boundaries. Agreed that the coverage can still be restricted or managed. Still, that control sits with a company operating from a foreign land.

On top of that, 100% foreign ownership is also spooking the authorities.

The technology is definitely useful and would help reduce the internet coverage gap FAST. But that would also open the door to misuse in places that India is most worried about, i.e., conflict zones, protests, and contested borders.

This is one of the sharpest test cases for satellite internet penetration in India, and it will be interesting to see how it plays out.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi Arrives in Washington for High-Stakes Meeting with President Trump 

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday night ahead of his 36-hour official visit to the United States. Modi is among the first foreign leaders to meet President Donald Trump since Trump assumed office as the 47th President of the United States.  

The visit is expected to focus on bilateral trade relations, with India seeking to avoid tariffs and strengthen economic ties with the U.S. Modi is set to meet President Trump at the White House on February 13 at 4:05 PM EST (2:35 AM IST on February 14). The meeting will take place in both restricted and delegation-level formats.  

During his 36-hour stay, Prime Minister Modi is scheduled to participate in six bilateral meetings. He is staying at Blair House, the U.S. presidential guest house located across from the White House.  

After the White House meeting, President Trump will host a private dinner for Modi in the evening.  

Prime Minister Modi is also expected to meet billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk during his visit. While no official confirmation has been made, sources familiar with the matter told Reuters that discussions could include Starlink's expansion into South Asia. Musk is reportedly expected to hold one-on-one talks with Modi if the meeting takes place.  

One of the key topics of discussion is expected to be Starlink's long-delayed entry into the Indian market. The Indian government anticipates discussions on satellite broadband services, as SpaceX's Starlink has been seeking approval to operate in India.  

Modi's visit marks a significant diplomatic engagement as both nations seek to strengthen their strategic and economic ties.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. text:
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has proposed making Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication systems mandatory for specified vehicles. V2V can improve road safety by allowing vehicles to exchange information such as speed, position and direction to prevent collisions. But an always-on system can also create a new infrastructure for tracking and surveillance. (1/5)
Read More: https://t.co/YckNaxIuq6

We have also raised concerns about centralised authentication systems. If a central authority can link a pseudonymous vehicle identifier back to a real vehicle, it could potentially reconstruct who is travelling where and when. Privacy should therefore be built into the technical architecture through decentralised systems, including technologies such as zero-knowledge credentials and secure hardware. (4/5)

IFF has urged MoRTH to ensure that V2V data cannot be centrally logged, intercepted, retained or repurposed for tracking, surveillance or law enforcement without specific legal authorisation and judicial oversight. Independent security and privacy audits should happen before mandatory deployment, followed by periodic reviews of whether the mandate remains necessary and proportionate. Safer roads should not mean building a new surveillance infrastructure. (5/5)

text: There is also a serious question about the databases being used. Delhi Police previously said facial recognition databases were maintained under a statute that Parliament has since repealed. Meanwhile, CP PLUS has publicly stated that it developed the Ikshana vehicle with Delhi Police. The legal basis for these databases, and what access private vendors have to facial data, remains unclear. (4/5)

Peaceful assembly is a constitutional right. Surveillance that identifies and profiles protesters can create a chilling effect on that right, especially when there are no clear rules, retention limits, privacy assessments or disclosed safeguards. The protest may have ended, but the question remains: where are the faces collected at Jantar Mantar now, who can access them, and under what law? (5/5)

The purpose of reserved names is to prevent impersonation of public institutions. “Sansad” is also an ordinary Hindi word, and “Chalo Sansad” was the reported name of a public protest. The website expressly disclaimed any affiliation with Parliament or the Government. Reserving https://t.co/vWkHekQQYB for the official Digital Sansad website does not mean citizens cannot lawfully refer to Parliament in a domain name. (7/8)

Today, acting on the registrant’s instructions, IFF through Apar Gupta, Advocate sent a rejoinder to NIXI. We have placed the inconsistencies, the 2004 policy, NIXI’s own reserved-name lists, the RDAP comparison and the Aadhaar concerns on record. We have again demanded restoration, disclosure of the legal basis and any underlying orders, accountability for the Aadhaar collected, and functional grievance channels. As of 17 August, https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP remains suspended. We will publish any further response. (8/8)

The government has all data on Aadhaar, Voter IDs, Passport so why is this information relevant for a census?

quotedTweet.text:
IFF has written to the Union Home Secretary and the Census Commissioner over the household survey notified four days ago. Serial numbers 36 to 40 ask for mobile, Aadhaar, voter ID and passport numbers, not whether you have them, unlike serial number 40, which only asks about availability of a driving license.

IFF supports enumerating caste for substantive equality. But pairing Aadhaar numbers with religion and caste sits against the Aadhaar Act's bar on profiling, and the questionnaire itself remains unpublished.
We are not opposed to the census. We want it conducted in a way that earns public trust.
